questions.sub: Concept of Milieu Interieur and Homeostasis
questions.q: Which nineteenth-century French physiologist first formulated the concept of the constancy of the internal environment (milieu interieur)?
options: Claude Bernard
Walter Bradford Cannon
Ernest Starling
Charles Sherrington
questions.explain: Claude Bernard introduced the concept of the milieu interieur (internal environment), stating that its constancy is the condition for free and independent life; Walter Cannon later coined the term homeostasis.

open.q: Name the French physiologist who originated the concept of the constancy of the internal environment (milieu interieur).

questions.sub: Concept of Milieu Interieur and Homeostasis
questions.q: Who coined the term homeostasis to describe the coordinated physiological processes that maintain steady states in the body?
options: Claude Bernard
Walter B. Cannon
William Harvey
Ivan Pavlov
questions.explain: Walter Bradford Cannon coined the word homeostasis in 1929 and described the role of the sympathoadrenal system in preserving internal stability during stress.

open.q: Name the American physiologist who coined the term homeostasis.

questions.sub: Concept of Milieu Interieur and Homeostasis
questions.q: Which body fluid compartment directly constitutes the immediate internal environment (milieu interieur) bathing most tissue cells?
options: Intracellular fluid
Transcellular fluid
Interstitial fluid
Cerebrospinal fluid
questions.explain: Interstitial fluid makes up roughly three-quarters of the extracellular fluid and directly surrounds tissue cells, exchanging nutrients, gases, and wastes across capillary walls and cell membranes.

open.q: Which subdivision of extracellular fluid directly surrounds tissue cells and serves as their immediate internal environment?

questions.sub: Concept of Milieu Interieur and Homeostasis
questions.q: Which statement best defines homeostasis in human physiology?
options: Total absence of fluctuations in any physiological variable at all times
Complete isolation of the organism from changes in the external environment
Permanent elevation of metabolic variables above baseline during activity
Maintenance of nearly constant conditions in the internal environment through dynamic regulatory responses
questions.explain: Homeostasis is a dynamic steady state rather than static equilibrium; physiological variables oscillate slightly around a set point as opposing effectors continuously correct deviations.

open.q: Define homeostasis in human physiology.
accept: Maintenance of a constant internal environment
Dynamic maintenance of steady internal conditions
Regulation of the internal environment within narrow limits

questions.sub: Components of a Homeostatic Control System
questions.q: In a physiological reflex arc, what is the role of the sensor (receptor)?
options: Detecting changes in a regulated variable and transmitting afferent signals to the control center
Comparing actual input against a stored reference value
Executing mechanical or secretory changes to alter the regulated variable
Generating hormones directly into the systemic venous circulation
questions.explain: Sensors (such as carotid sinus baroreceptors or hypothalamic osmoreceptors) transduce changes in a regulated variable into afferent neural or humoral signals sent to an integrating center.

open.q: What is the primary function of the sensor (receptor) in a homeostatic control loop?
accept: Detects changes in a regulated variable and sends afferent signals
Monitors the controlled variable and informs the integrating center

questions.sub: Components of a Homeostatic Control System
questions.q: Which component of a homeostatic feedback loop compares incoming afferent information with the set point and coordinates an appropriate output?
options: Peripheral transducer
Integrating (control) center
Effector organ
Efferent target tissue
questions.explain: The integrating center (often located in the hypothalamus, brainstem, or an endocrine gland) evaluates afferent error signals relative to the set point and dispatches efferent commands to effectors.

open.q: Name the component of a homeostatic control system that compares afferent input against the set point and initiates efferent output.

questions.sub: Components of a Homeostatic Control System
questions.q: What is the error signal in a physiological feedback control system?
options: The maximum possible output capacity of an effector organ
A structural mutation in a membrane hormone receptor
The difference between the actual measured value of a variable and its set point
The time delay required for an action potential to cross a synapse
questions.explain: An error signal equals the discrepancy between the sensed value of a controlled variable and the desired set point; it drives the proportional response of the integrating center.

open.q: In control system physiology, what does the term error signal refer to?
accept: Difference between actual value and set point
Deviation of a regulated variable from its set point

questions.q: How does a negative feedback mechanism stabilize a physiological variable?
options: By amplifying the initial deviation in the same direction until a climax occurs
By permanently shutting down all effector organs once a stimulus appears
By anticipating disturbances before any change occurs in the blood
By initiating an effector response that opposes and reduces the initial deviation from the set point
questions.explain: Negative feedback produces a response opposite in direction to the initiating disturbance, restoring the regulated variable back toward its normal set point.

open.q: How does a negative feedback loop respond to a deviation in a regulated physiological variable?
accept: It opposes the initial change to restore the set point
It reverses the direction of the disturbance

questions.q: Which physiological process is a classic example of negative feedback control?
options: Suppression of pituitary TSH secretion by rising plasma thyroxine (T4) levels
Oxytocin-induced uterine contractions during active labor
Rapid sodium influx driving the upstroke of a neuronal action potential
Activation of clotting factors during the coagulation cascade
questions.explain: Elevated circulating thyroid hormones inhibit TRH and TSH release from the hypothalamus and anterior pituitary, lowering thyroid stimulation back toward normal; labor contractions, action potential depolarization, and clotting are positive feedback loops.

open.q: Explain why the regulation of thyroid hormone secretion via TSH is classified as negative feedback.
accept: High thyroid hormone inhibits TSH release to reduce further hormone synthesis
Elevated T3 and T4 suppress pituitary TSH secretion

questions.q: A rise in arterial blood pressure stretches baroreceptors in the carotid sinus and aortic arch, leading to reflex bradycardia and arteriolar vasodilation. Why is this reflex classified as negative feedback?
options: Because heart rate decreases rather than increases
Because the combined cardiovascular response lowers arterial pressure back toward its set point
Because parasympathetic nerve firing inhibits sympathetic ganglia directly
Because baroreceptors adapt completely within seconds of pressure elevation
questions.explain: Negative feedback is defined by the direction of the effect on the regulated variable relative to the initial perturbation: an initial rise in blood pressure triggers responses that decrease blood pressure.

open.q: Why is the arterial baroreceptor reflex triggered by acute hypertension classified as a negative feedback mechanism?
accept: The reflex lowers arterial blood pressure back toward normal
Its output opposes the initial increase in blood pressure

questions.q: A physiological control system with a gain of -9 experiences a disturbance that would change arterial pressure by +20 mmHg if no compensation occurred. What is the resulting change in arterial pressure after compensation?
options: +18 mmHg (plus 18 mmHg)
+10 mmHg (plus 10 mmHg)
+2 mmHg (plus 2 mmHg)
-2 mmHg (minus 2 mmHg)
questions.explain: Gain = Correction / Remaining Error. With |Gain| = 9, Correction = 9 * Remaining Error, and Total Disturbance = Correction + Remaining Error = 10 * Remaining Error; thus Remaining Error = +20 / 10 = +2 mmHg.

open.q: If an uncompensated disturbance would raise a regulated variable by 20 units and the control system has a negative feedback gain of -9, what is the final residual error after compensation?

questions.q: Which physiological homeostatic mechanism possesses virtually infinite gain over long periods?
options: Arterial baroreceptor reflex
Pupillary light reflex
Chemoreceptor control of ventilation
Renal-body fluid pressure control system
questions.explain: The renal-body fluid mechanism (pressure natriuresis and diuresis) continues adjusting extracellular fluid volume until arterial pressure returns all the way to its exact equilibrium point, leaving zero steady-state error and effectively infinite gain.

open.q: Name the long-term blood pressure regulatory mechanism that exhibits virtually infinite negative feedback gain.

questions.q: Which statement accurately describes a physiological positive feedback mechanism?
options: The output reinforces and amplifies the initial stimulus in the same direction until a discrete endpoint terminates the cycle
It always indicates fatal organ decompensation and never serves a normal bodily function
It is the primary mechanism maintaining resting blood glucose and core body temperature
It dampens oscillations in plasma calcium concentration within narrow limits
questions.explain: Positive feedback amplifies an initial change in the same direction; although uncontrolled positive feedback causes vicious cycles (such as hemorrhagic shock), controlled positive feedback drives essential biological events like parturition, ovulation, and action potentials.

open.q: How does a positive feedback mechanism differ from negative feedback in its effect on an initial stimulus?
accept: It amplifies or reinforces the initial stimulus in the same direction
It enhances rather than opposes the initial change

questions.q: During parturition, stretching of the uterine cervix stimulates posterior pituitary oxytocin release, which increases uterine contractions and further stretches the cervix. What event finally terminates this positive feedback cycle?
options: Depletion of all maternal oxytocin stores in the hypothalamus
Expulsion (delivery) of the fetus, removing cervical stretch
Sudden progesterone surge from the placenta
Complete desensitization of uterine smooth muscle to calcium
questions.explain: The Ferguson reflex is a self-limiting positive feedback loop that ends abruptly when delivery of the baby eliminates mechanical stretch on the uterine cervix.

open.q: What external physiological event terminates the positive feedback loop of oxytocin release during childbirth (the Ferguson reflex)?

questions.q: Which reproductive endocrine event relies on positive feedback by high sustained levels of estradiol on the anterior pituitary?
options: Inhibition of FSH during the early follicular phase
Suppression of GnRH pulsatility during lactation
The mid-cycle luteinizing hormone (LH) surge triggering ovulation
Progesterone-mediated quiescence of the myometrium in pregnancy
questions.explain: When estradiol remains elevated above threshold for 36 to 48 hours late in the follicular phase, its effect on hypothalamic-pituitary gonadotrophs switches from negative to positive feedback, producing the preovulatory LH surge.

open.q: Which preovulatory hormonal event is triggered by positive feedback from sustained high estradiol levels?

questions.q: A trauma patient loses 2.2 liters of blood, causing arterial pressure to fall so low that coronary blood flow drops and myocardial contractility weakens, further lowering arterial pressure. This clinical deterioration illustrates which principle?
options: Feedforward anticipatory adaptation
High-gain negative feedback compensation
Circadian resetting of the baroreceptor set point
Decompensating vicious cycle of positive feedback
questions.explain: Beyond a critical threshold of blood loss, negative feedback mechanisms are overwhelmed and severe hypotension impairs cardiac pumping, creating a self-amplifying positive feedback spiral into irreversible hemorrhagic shock.

open.q: In severe hemorrhagic shock, falling arterial pressure reduces coronary perfusion, which further weakens cardiac output and lowers pressure even more. What control system phenomenon does this represent?

questions.q: What is the defining feature of feedforward (adaptive) control in physiology?
options: Initiating corrective responses in anticipation of a disturbance before the regulated variable actually changes
Waiting until a variable exceeds toxic thresholds before activating effectors
Amplifying a blood electrolyte disturbance until renal failure occurs
Eliminating the need for any central nervous system involvement
questions.explain: Feedforward control predicts an impending perturbation using sensory cues (such as sight, smell, or GI distension) and activates effectors preemptively to minimize fluctuations in the internal environment.

open.q: How does feedforward control prevent large disturbances in a regulated physiological variable?
accept: It initiates anticipatory responses before the variable changes
It acts preemptively in anticipation of a disturbance

questions.q: Which physiological response is an example of feedforward regulation?
options: Secretion of aldosterone in response to hyperkalemia
Cephalic-phase insulin and gastric acid secretion triggered by the sight and smell of food before blood glucose rises
Release of antidiuretic hormone (ADH) after plasma osmolarity increases to 300 mOsm/L
Parathyroid hormone secretion following a drop in ionized plasma calcium
questions.explain: Seeing, smelling, or tasting food triggers vagally mediated insulin and gastric secretion before nutrients are absorbed into the bloodstream, blunting the subsequent postprandial glucose spike.

open.q: Give an example of feedforward control involving digestion and blood glucose regulation when a person sees or smells food.
accept: Anticipatory insulin release before food absorption

questions.q: At the very onset of dynamic exercise, pulmonary ventilation increases abruptly within seconds even before arterial PCO2, PO2, or pH have changed. Which regulatory mechanism accounts for this immediate hyperpnea?
options: Central chemoreceptor stimulation by CSF acidosis
Peripheral chemoreceptor activation by arterial hypoxemia
Feedforward neural signals from motor cortex collaterals and joint proprioceptors
Renal bicarbonate excretion altering blood pH
questions.explain: Central command from the motor cortex and afferent feedback from moving limb proprioceptors stimulate the medullary respiratory center immediately at exercise onset in a feedforward manner, keeping arterial blood gases remarkably constant.

open.q: What regulatory mechanism drives the immediate rise in ventilation at the start of exercise before arterial blood gases change?
accept: Central command and proprioceptive feedforward signals

questions.q: During a bacterial infection, endogenous pyrogens act on the hypothalamus to produce fever. What happens to the thermoregulatory control system during the chill (onset) phase of fever?
options: The hypothalamic set point drops to 35 C while skin blood vessels dilate
Negative feedback is permanently destroyed and replaced by positive feedback
Sweat glands are maximally stimulated despite normal core temperature
The hypothalamic set point is elevated to a higher temperature, causing the body to conserve and generate heat via shivering
questions.explain: Prostaglandin E2 raises the hypothalamic thermoregulatory set point (e.g., to 39 C); because actual blood temperature is initially lower than the new set point, the body perceives itself as cold and triggers cutaneous vasoconstriction and shivering.

open.q: In terms of homeostatic control systems, what happens to the hypothalamic thermoregulatory set point during the onset of fever?
accept: The set point is raised to a higher temperature
Elevation of the hypothalamic set point

questions.q: Which hypothalamic nucleus acts as the master circadian pacemaker generating 24-hour rhythms in cortisol secretion, core body temperature, and sleep-wake cycles?
options: Suprachiasmatic nucleus
Supraoptic nucleus
Arcuate nucleus
Ventromedial nucleus
questions.explain: The suprachiasmatic nucleus (SCN) receives direct photic input from the retina via the retinohypothalamic tract and entrains daily rhythmic shifts in physiological set points.

open.q: Name the hypothalamic nucleus that serves as the master circadian clock regulating 24-hour physiological rhythms.

questions.q: What mode of intercellular signaling occurs when a cell secretes a chemical messenger into the interstitial fluid that acts only on neighboring target cells without entering the bloodstream?
options: Endocrine signaling
Paracrine signaling
Autocrine signaling
Neuroendocrine signaling
questions.explain: Paracrine mediators (such as histamine, nitric oxide, or somatostatin in pancreatic islets) diffuse locally through interstitial fluid to regulate nearby cells and are rapidly inactivated before reaching systemic circulation.

open.q: Name the type of local chemical signaling in which a messenger diffuses through interstitial fluid to act on adjacent target cells.

questions.q: When an activated T lymphocyte secretes interleukin-2 that binds to receptors on the very same T cell to stimulate its own proliferation, which signaling mechanism is operating?
options: Juxtacrine signaling
Endocrine signaling
Autocrine signaling
Synaptic signaling
questions.explain: Autocrine signaling occurs when a cell releases a ligand that binds to receptors on its own plasma membrane to self-regulate its activity.

open.q: What term describes intercellular communication in which a secreted chemical messenger acts on receptors on the same cell that released it?

questions.q: Why are vital homeostatic variables such as arterial blood pressure and plasma glucose regulated by multiple overlapping control systems rather than a single mechanism?
options: To ensure all hormones are secreted at identical rates throughout the day
Because single feedback loops cannot operate in extracellular fluid
To eliminate all neural input from the autonomic nervous system
To provide functional redundancy and cover both rapid short-term corrections and sustained long-term stability
questions.explain: Multiple overlapping mechanisms (such as fast neural baroreceptors, intermediate hormonal renin-angiotensin-aldosterone, and slow renal fluid control) operate across different time scales and provide backup if one system fails.

open.q: State two physiological advantages of regulating critical variables like blood pressure with multiple overlapping homeostatic systems.
accept: Redundancy and coverage across short-term and long-term time scales
Backup protection if one system fails and fast plus slow regulation

questions.q: A 55-year-old man with untreated chronic hypertension (baseline BP 170/105 mmHg) has normal resting heart rate because his carotid sinus baroreceptors have adapted to fire at a normal baseline rate at 170 mmHg. Which homeostatic phenomenon explains this adaptation?
options: Baroreceptor resetting of the operating set point
Complete failure of negative feedback gain
Feedforward inhibition of the vasomotor center
Autocrine downregulation of cardiac beta receptors
questions.explain: Within 1 to 2 days of sustained pressure elevation, arterial baroreceptors reset their firing threshold to the higher pressure level, defending the new hypertensive set point against acute fluctuations rather than returning pressure to 120/80 mmHg.

open.q: What physiological phenomenon causes arterial baroreceptors to adapt within 1 to 2 days to a chronically elevated blood pressure?
